result.summary: Interpreted the quantified impact receipt (911dce1c4a2849d4a868d72c50403c78, exit 0, both cases passed): all five comparisons are complete and hold, so the replay effect and its cost are decided — one identical TimeoutNow payload honoured a second time raised the term (3 -> 4), one client write out of 138 attempts was refused with 'node is not the leader' at the first step (refusal window shorter than one 10 ms step), one sample in 138 showed no leader, and the control's plain campaign stayed refused with no leadership change. That account is recorded with all three receipts cited, keeping the bounded impact and the unchanged leader identity explicit. While reading further I also traced the network transport's heartbeat fast path: it calls the raft handler inline on the connection goroutine (net_transport.go 721-727), applies only to pure heartbeats (whose request carries no previous entry and no commit index), and therefore touches only lock-protected or atomic state — so the concurrency concern is narrower than the two contradictory comments (api.go 625-632 versus raft.go 1433-1436) suggest. The remaining question in those paths is registered as @q_stale_heartbeat_stepdown with a source-based, unresolved account: appendEntries moves any non-follower to Follower and adopts the message's term whenever the term is greater or the node is not already a follower, so a stale leader's heartbeat could depose the current leader and persist a lower term; its discriminator is a three-voter cluster with two leaders of different terms that can still exchange heartbeats, recorded as the next step. investigations.hypothesis: TimeoutNowRequest embeds only the RPC header, and timeoutNow clears the known leader, becomes a candidate and sets the leadership-transfer flag without inspecting term, sender identity or configuration, while the flag in the request's vote messages bypasses the known-leader rejection. investigations.discriminator: The two-case receipt: in the duplicate case the term after the duplicate delivery exceeds the term after the first transfer and the leadership set is recorded again, while the control case records an ungranted plain vote, an unchanged term and no leadership change. investigations.question: Does an AppendEntries message whose term is older than the receiver's still move a non-follower to Follower and write the older term into the stable store, and can a stale leader's heartbeat therefore depose the current leader and lower its persisted term?
investigations.hypothesis: In appendEntries the term/state transition fires on `a.Term > r.getCurrentTerm() || (r.getState() != Follower && !candidateFromLeadershipTransfer.Load())`, and the second disjunct ignores the term entirely, so a message with an older term still sets Follower and calls setCurrentTerm(a.Term) - persisting a lower term. The heartbeat goroutine's request carries no previous entry and no leader commit index, which is exactly the condition the network transport uses for its inline fast path, so a stale leader's heartbeat reaches this transition without any log content to reject it.
investigations.discriminator: A three-voter cluster in which one voter is partitioned early, keeps believing it leads, and later exchanges heartbeats with a healthy current leader of a higher term: record that leader's state and its persisted current term before and after the stale message, then check whether the stale leader can win the resulting election. If the current leader keeps leader state and its persisted term is unchanged, the suspicion is refuted; if it steps down with a lower persisted term, the effect is established and the follow-on question is whether the stale leader's log can then win.

interpretations.rationale: Present conclusion: the phantom log claim produced by the InstallSnapshot path changes how a server decides votes, because requestVote evaluates log completeness with getLastEntry, which prefers the cached claim over the installed snapshot. Source basis: getLastEntry returns (lastLogIndex,lastLogTerm) whenever lastLogIndex >= lastSnapshotIndex (src_get_last_entry, state.go 160-174); requestVote's completeness test rejects only when the voter's last term is greater than the candidate's, or equal with a greater index (src_vote_log_check, raft.go 1725-1748 inside requestVote at 1626-1758); installSnapshot never resets that cached entry (src_install_snapshot_tail, raft.go 1837-1977). Consequence: a voter whose snapshot already contains committed entries in a newer term will still grant a vote to a candidate whose last log entry carries an older term, whenever the cached claim wins the comparison - exactly the case a voter comparing against its snapshot would reject. The scope is bounded rather than established as a safety break: the phantom suffix was never committed (a quorum storing it would have committed it), so its holders were a minority of the configuration that created it, and a leader's snapshot index cannot fall below committed history; a quorum of phantom voters therefore needs a configuration change that turns that minority into a majority of a new configuration. The affected direction is also milder than the phrasing 'stale rejection' suggests: the claim can both reject candidates whose last term equals the claimed term with a lower index and grant candidates whose last term is below the snapshot's term. Limits: this account is source-derived plus local construction feedback (the five-voter probe behaved as predicted: phantom granted, consistent voter rejected, candidate term below the phantom's snapshot term); it has no retained receipt yet, the vote effect is unmeasured in 3-voter configurations, and the configuration-change path that could turn phantom holders into a quorum is not measured at all.
counterevidence: The same root cause in the progress direction was measured to be bounded: starvation ends once a snapshot above the cached claim is published (parent question receipt), so the phantom claim is a transient state within a term, not a permanent log corruption.

That protective side also bounds the safety reading: the steps that would shrink the voter set down to the phantom group cannot commit, so the phantom grant cannot be converted into authority over committed entries through configuration changes in the measured history. Limits: the wedge and the corrected config-change comparisons await their receipt (currently construction feedback and raw retained values respectively); configuration changes attempted before the phantom state arises, repeated phantom generations, other cluster sizes and production-style monotonic stores are unmeasured; the leader's reported configuration size after a blocked change reflects the locally adopted latest configuration, not the committed one.

interpretations.rationale: Present conclusion: the leadership-transfer control message carries no term and no sender-role information, and its handler validates nothing, so a duplicate or delayed copy is honoured exactly like a fresh one and forces another election in an otherwise healthy cluster. Source basis: TimeoutNowRequest embeds only RPCHeader (src_timeout_now_msg, commands.go 205-208), and timeoutNow clears the known leader, moves the node to Candidate and sets the candidate-from-transfer flag before responding (src_timeout_now, raft.go 2232-2239); that flag is what makes voters skip the known-leader rejection in requestVote (src_request_vote, raft.go 1626-1758, known-leader check at 1671-1680). Local construction runs of the new probe show the expected contrast in a three-voter cluster with ten committed entries: the first delivery moved leadership to the target (term 2 -> 3) and the identical payload delivered again to that new leader raised the term again to 4 while it stayed Leader, whereas the control's plain follower campaign with the same log claim was not granted, left the term at 2 and changed no leadership. Limits: the receipt is requested with this update; the probe delivers the message through another node's transport, which is the same path a middleware or delayed delivery would use, and it does not measure a partition during the replay, larger clusters, or the duration of the leadership gap caused by the second election.
counterevidence: The first delivery is the documented transfer path and is expected behaviour; only the second, identical delivery is the defect subject, and it is supplied by the harness rather than produced by the library's own transport.

Raft tolerates spurious elections for safety; the harm here is the avoidable term churn, the leadership gap while the target campaigns, and the loss of the current leader's stability, not a stale leader's log being elected.
limitations: No retained receipt yet; the effect is currently shown by local construction runs of the requested experiment.
One delivery path and cluster size; the leadership gap and any interaction with partitions or in-flight writes are unmeasured.

interpretations.rationale: Present conclusion: the source shows that appendEntries moves any non-follower to Follower and adopts the message's term whenever the message term is greater OR the node is not already a follower (src_append_prev_check, raft.go 1458-1606, transition block around 1478-1489), and the heartbeat goroutine's request carries only the header, term and leader address (src_heartbeat_req, replication.go 388-412), so a stale leader's heartbeat is not filtered by any log content. Two narrower facts bound the concern: the network transport's inline fast path applies exactly to such pure heartbeats (src_net_heartbeat_fastpath, net_transport.go 655-730, with the fast-path condition at 671-676 and the inline call at 721-727) and those messages touch only lock-protected or atomic state (leader identity, state, term, last contact), because the same request shape carries no previous entry and no leader commit index, which skips the log, configuration and commit paths; and the api.go comment asserts the handler must be safe to call concurrently (src_fastpath_contract, api.go 625-632) while the handler's own comment says it must only be called from the main thread (raft.go 1433-1436), a contradiction whose reconciliation is that the pure-heartbeat path mutates only guarded fields. What remains open is the transition itself: an older-term message arriving at a leader makes that leader a follower and persists the older term, which a stale leader's heartbeat can deliver. No observation yet shows a leader stepping down or a persisted term decreasing, so the defect judgment is unresolved rather than asserted, and the discriminator above is the requested next step. Limits: the transition is shared with the normal (non-fast-path) delivery, so any effect is not fast-path specific; nothing here shows whether a stale leader's log could then win, and the term-regression direction would have to be checked against the vote records, which are persisted separately.
counterevidence: The same transition exists on the normal main-thread path, so it is not introduced by the concurrency the fast-path comments argue about.
The fast-path heartbeats carry no log content, so they cannot corrupt logs, configurations or the FSM; only the state, term, leader identity and last-contact fields can change.
No observation yet shows the effect: the suspicion rests on source reading only.
limitations: Unobserved: the probe described as the discriminator has not been run, so both the step-down and any persisted term regression are unconfirmed.
Reachability requires two leaders of different terms that can still exchange heartbeats, which no measurement here has constructed.
